summary: Mary hurries to Elizabeth, whose unborn son leaps at her greeting; Elizabeth blesses Mary as mother of her Lord, and Mary sings praise to God her Savior.
key_insight: The first person in Luke to call Jesus “Lord” is an older woman speaking of a child not yet born: “the mother of my Lord.” And the first to respond to Him is John, leaping in the womb for joy, already doing what he was born to do.
story: Soon after Gabriel’s visit, Mary set out and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah. She entered the house of Zacharias and greeted Elizabeth.

When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. She cried out with a loud voice, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! But why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” The baby, she said, had leaped for joy at the sound of Mary’s voice. “Blessed is she who believed, for there will be a fulfillment of those things which were told her from the Lord.”

Mary answered with a song of praise: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior.” God had regarded the lowly state of His maidservant, and from now on all generations would call her blessed. “He who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is His name.”

Then her song turned from what God had done for her to what He does in the world. His mercy is on those who fear Him from generation to generation. He has scattered the proud. “He has put down the mighty from their thrones, and exalted the lowly. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich He has sent away empty.”
He has helped His servant Israel, remembering the mercy He promised to Abraham and his descendants forever. Mary stayed with Elizabeth about three months, and then returned to her own home.

scene.label: The journey
scene.text: Luke names only “a city of Judah” in the hill country. Tradition places Zacharias’s home at Ain Karim, a few miles west of Jerusalem, but no one knows for certain. From Nazareth, any town in the Judean hills was a journey of several days on foot.

scene.label: Hannah’s song
scene.text: Mary’s song closely echoes Hannah’s prayer when she gave Samuel to the Lord (1 Samuel 2:1–10): “He brings low and lifts up” (1 Samuel 2:7). Nearly every line of Mary’s song draws on older Scripture, the words of a young woman who knew her Bible well.

scene.label: The Magnificat
scene.text: The song is called the Magnificat, from its first word in Latin, “magnifies.” The church has sung or prayed it for centuries, and it stands first among the songs Luke records around Jesus’ birth.

scene.label: Three months
scene.text: Elizabeth was six months pregnant when Mary arrived (1:36), so Mary stayed until about the time of John’s birth. Luke mentions her return before he tells of the birth, perhaps to finish Mary’s part of the story; he does not say whether she was there for it.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records the meeting of the two mothers and Mary’s song. He loves to show the Holy Spirit at work and to record praise, and the Magnificat announces a theme he returns to again and again: the lowly lifted and the proud brought down, as in Jesus’ blessings and woes (Luke 6:20–26).

seeing.reveals: Even before His birth, Jesus is “Lord,” and His coming means mercy for the humble and the overthrow of the proud. Mary’s Son is the fulfillment of the mercy God promised to Abraham.
seeing.living: Elizabeth had waited a lifetime for her own son, yet she rejoiced that a young relative had received the greater honor. Her son would later say of Jesus, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). When God lifts someone else higher, bless them as Elizabeth did.
seeing.ponder: When God honors someone else more than you, can you rejoice with them as Elizabeth did?

preaching.big_idea: God lifts the lowly who trust Him and brings down the proud who trust themselves.
outline: A meeting filled with the Spirit (39–45)
A soul that magnifies the Lord (46–50)
A God who turns the world upside down (51–53)
preaching.watch_for: Mary speaks of God’s great reversals in the past tense: He “has scattered,” “has put down,” “has filled.” She speaks of what God will do as already done, because in the Child she carries He has already begun it.
